newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Italy, Spain on track to join euro - Matutes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy, Spain on track to join euro - Matutes.

text.p: Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said on Tuesday that Spain and Italy were on course to join Economic and Monetary Union from the start, dismissing fears that political factors could prevent them from joining.

"Italy has shown its willingness to make the necessary adjustments to meet the (Maastricht) criteria," Matutes told a news conference during a trip to Lisbon. "I think that for the time being it will be capable of doing so," he added.

"Spain has every probability of joining the first stage of Economic and Monetary Union," he said. "This government is firmly committed to meeting the Maastricht criteria, which are the only conditions that will determine which countries will join this union in its first stage and which will not."

Matutes was responding to concerns in financial markets that the so-called "Club Med" countries, including Italy, Spain and Portugal, may not qualify to join the European single currency, or euro, on January 1, 1999.

Portuguese Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco told a parliamentary commission on Tuesday he was confident Portugal would join the euro in 1999 and played down remarks by a German official who said some states were not ready to take part.
"This is a political game," Sousa Franco said. "The industrialists of Germany and others are very frightened of Italy joining the euro," he added.

He was referring to remarks last week by Juergen Stark, the number two at Germany's Finance Ministry, who made clear that some countries which qualified for EMU should stay outside for a time after 1999.

Stark did not name any countries, but there was little doubt he meant southern EU members like Spain and Italy when he said some countries which qualify on paper "would be well advised to maintain exchange rate flexibility for a certain period."
Spanish financial markets tumbled on Monday as jubilance over economic accomplishments gave way to dismay that political factors might prevent it from joining the launch of the euro.

Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar had focused the nation's EMU drive on its economic accomplishments, in an attempt to disengage Spain's political status from the more politically powerful but economically weak Italy.

But the EU's power brokers clearly are finding it difficult to exclude Italy, a founding member of the European Union and a Group of Seven member, while admitting the lesser power, Spain -- regardless of its paper credentials.
Matutes said he believed the more nations that qualified to join the euro, the better.
"I think it is good if a large number of countries meet the (EMU) conditions," he said, flanked by Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama.
Matutes said he and Gama had discussed a range of bilateral and international security issues during his visit.
